provenance.source_title: Towards Attuned AI: Integrating Care Ethics in Large Language Model Development and Alignment

research_problem.text: How can the ethics of care inform LLM development and value alignment when existing approaches inadequately address individual circumstances, vulnerability, and relational context?

central_claims.text: Mainstream AI alignment frameworks frequently overlook situated, affective, and power-sensitive dimensions of moral life.

evidence.text: While mainstream AI alignment methods often draw from utilitarian or deontological principles, these frameworks frequently overlook the situated, affective, and power-sensitive dimensions of moral life that EoC brings to the foreground.
evidence.locator: 1.1 Introduction

central_claims.text: Integrating care ethics into LLM design and value alignment offers a richer, more contextually grounded normative foundation.

evidence.text: We argue that integrating care ethics into the design and value alignment (VA) processes of LLMs offers a richer and more contextually grounded normative foundation for generative AI systems.
evidence.locator: 1.1 Introduction

central_claims.text: The authors regard the ethics of care as a necessary ethical foundation for the future responsible development of LLMs, not merely a relevant option.

evidence.text: Through our two arguments, one from the dissonance of LLM's generalizations and another from the shortcomings of current normative frameworks, we aim to show why EoC is not only a relevant but necessary ethical foundation for the future of responsible LLMs' development.
evidence.locator: 1.2 Introducing the Ethics of Care

central_claims.text: Because the real world is dynamic and difficult to represent as a static training distribution, performance on apparent edge cases is crucial to assessing LLM generalization.

evidence.text: The 'real world' where LLMs operate is rarely as neatly categorized as a static training distribution might suggest.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

evidence.text: Consequently, the performance of FFNNs in these seemingly 'edge' scenarios becomes a crucial consideration, highlighting a significant gap between theoretical capabilities within controlled distributions and the unpredictable nature of real-world applications.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

central_claims.text: LLMs are vulnerable to the generalization problems of feed-forward neural networks and frequently produce biased, context-insensitive, or inappropriate outputs.

evidence.text: As such, they are vulnerable to the same generalization problems. We see this in practice through empirical evidence that LLMs frequently exhibit representational biases and produce context-insensitive or inappropriate outputs, a problem extensively documented in recent work [Navigli et al., 2023].
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

central_claims.text: Continuing to build systems dependent on rules that fail to generalize appropriately is ethically and functionally problematic.

evidence.text: If LLMs in practice rely on complex rules to apply knowledge to new contexts, rules which often fail to generalize appropriately in practice, then continuing to build systems that depend on such generalization is ethically and functionally problematic.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

central_claims.text: The authors cite discriminatory therapy-chatbot responses, gender-stereotyped storytelling, and biased benefit assessments as examples of harmful bias in care-relevant applications.

evidence.text: In the realm of mental health, research has shown therapy chatbots exhibiting discriminatory responses based on users' conditions, perpetuating harmful stigmas [Harrison Dupre, 2025]. Regarding gender, LLMs have been found to generate narratives that reinforce traditional stereotypes in storytelling, demonstrating a clear gender bias in creative outputs [UCL, 2024]. Furthermore, in the context of social services, attempts to implement AI for fairer benefit assessments have resulted in the reproduction of existing human biases, highlighting the challenge of achieving equitable outcomes through purely algorithmic means [Guo et al., 2024].
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

central_claims.text: Bias in aligned LLMs arises not only from training data but also from subjective values in human and AI feedback.

evidence.text: This bias is not solely a product of flawed training data but also arises from the subjective values embedded in human and even AI feedback during alignment processes.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

central_claims.text: Moral frameworks prioritizing abstract utility or generalized fairness are inadequate for addressing the nuanced biases the authors identify.

evidence.text: Consequently, relying on dominant moral frameworks that prioritize abstract utility or generalized fairness proves inadequate for addressing these nuanced biases.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

central_claims.text: LLM training and design should prioritize individual and contextual particularities rather than statistical generalization; this shift could mitigate harms from misapplied generalizations.

evidence.text: Re-thinking the training and design of LLMs through the lens of EoC would entail prioritizing individual and contextual particularities rather than optimizing for statistical generalization. This shift could help mitigate the harmful consequences of misapplied generalizations and align AI systems more closely with the nuanced moral demands of human interaction.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the dissonance of LLM generalizations

central_claims.text: RLHF and RLAIF embody utilitarian and justice-based normative commitments rather than being value-neutral techniques.

evidence.text: Current Value Alignment (VA) methods, particularly Reinforcement Learning from Human Feedback (RLHF) and its more recent variant Reinforcement Learning from AI Feedback (RLAIF), are grounded in specific normative frameworks, primarily utilitarianism and justice-based theories such as Contractualism and Rawlsian justice.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the Shortcomings of Current Normative Commitments of VA methods in Care-Related Contexts

evidence.text: These moral commitments, however, are not value-neutral.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the Shortcomings of Current Normative Commitments of VA methods in Care-Related Contexts

central_claims.text: Utilitarian alignment can justify sacrificing an individual's well-being for aggregate benefit, which is ethically troubling in care-relevant settings.

evidence.text: Utilitarian approaches may justify sacrificing individual well-being for the sake of aggregated good, which is ethically troubling in contexts such as mental health or healthcare, where individual vulnerability and situational complexity demand more than mere utility maximization [Sola, 2023].
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the Shortcomings of Current Normative Commitments of VA methods in Care-Related Contexts

central_claims.text: Justice-based alignment can overemphasize truthfulness or impartiality at the expense of individuals' emotional, relational, and contextual needs.

evidence.text: Likewise, justice-based approaches may overemphasize principles such as truthfulness or impartiality, and fail to account for the emotional, relational, and context-sensitive needs of individuals in morally complex or care-relevant situations [Gilligan, 1993].
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the Shortcomings of Current Normative Commitments of VA methods in Care-Related Contexts

central_claims.text: Current alignment frameworks based on rule-following and aggregation prove inadequate in settings where unique, emotionally laden, context-dependent needs make care central.

evidence.text: Examples include healthcare, education, eldercare, and mental health support, these fields in which the needs of individuals are unique, emotionally laden, and highly context-dependent [Beauchamp, 2006]. In such settings, the current VA frameworks, grounded in rule-following and aggregation, prove inadequate.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the Shortcomings of Current Normative Commitments of VA methods in Care-Related Contexts

central_claims.text: Anthropic's Constitutional AI presents a deontological stance but operates through utilitarian, reward-maximizing mechanics; the authors say its technical implementation could only be utilitarian.

evidence.text: Thus, Anthropic's framework presents a deontological front, but its mechanics operate on utilitarian principles.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the Shortcomings of Current Normative Commitments of VA methods in Care-Related Contexts

evidence.text: As we have seen, although in principle, Anthropic adopted a deontological approach to value alignment, the technical implementation could only be utilitarian.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the Shortcomings of Current Normative Commitments of VA methods in Care-Related Contexts

central_claims.text: It is necessary to develop a care-ethics-inspired value alignment method tailored to care-relevant domains and contexts.

evidence.text: Therefore, we argue that it is necessary to develop a value alignment method tailored to care-relevant domains and contexts inspired by the ethics of care.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the Shortcomings of Current Normative Commitments of VA methods in Care-Related Contexts

central_claims.text: Genuinely aligning AI with human values, especially where people are vulnerable, necessitates adopting ethical frameworks such as care ethics that are rooted in lived moral experience.

evidence.text: In this paper, we have argued that the development of AI systems genuinely aligned with human values, especially within contexts involving human vulnerabilities, necessitates the adoption of ethical frameworks such as care ethics, which are deeply rooted in the moral realities of lived experiences.
evidence.locator: 2, An argument from the Shortcomings of Current Normative Commitments of VA methods in Care-Related Contexts

central_claims.text: A care-based alignment approach would train LLMs to attend morally to users' emotional, social, and contextual needs, rather than merely respond to reward signals.

evidence.text: A care-based VA approach would train systems not merely to be reward-sensitive, but to be morally attentive, i.e. responsive to the emotional, social, and contextual needs of users.
evidence.locator: 3 Conclusion

central_claims.text: Care ethics would guide alignment methods such as RLAIF to consider relational context and potential harms to vulnerable people and communities.

evidence.text: Rather than optimizing for abstract utility or procedural fairness, care ethics would guide alignment processes like RLAIF to consider the specific relational context and potential harms to vulnerable individuals and communities.
evidence.locator: 3 Conclusion

central_claims.text: Care ethics would inform human labelers to consider the broader relational impacts of AI responses, especially for marginalized or care-dependent populations.

evidence.text: It would also inform the work of human labelers, encouraging them to reflect not only on individual preferences, but on the broader relational impacts of AI responses, especially for marginalized or care-dependent populations.
evidence.locator: 3 Conclusion

central_claims.text: Care ethics could enrich constitutional alignment by promoting the well-being of caregivers and care-receivers within interdependent social networks.

evidence.text: Constitutionally, care ethics could provide a richer moral foundation by promoting the well-being of both caregivers and care-receivers within interdependent social networks.
evidence.locator: 3 Conclusion

central_claims.text: Embedding a care-based moral orientation would make LLM chatbots more likely to resist sycophancy, minimize hallucinations, and engage users with greater responsibility and trust.

evidence.text: By embedding this moral orientation, LLM's chatbots would be more likely to resist sycophantic behaviour, minimize hallucinations, and engage users with a deeper sense of responsibility and trust.
evidence.locator: 3 Conclusion

central_claims.text: Care ethics better reflects how people actually want to be treated in morally significant interactions with AI.

evidence.text: By offering a context-sensitive and relationally grounded framework, care ethics better reflects how people actually want to be treated in morally significant interactions with AI.
evidence.locator: 3 Conclusion

methodology.summary: Conceptual argument drawing on care ethics, literature on LLM generalization and bias, and analysis of the normative assumptions and mechanisms of RLHF, RLAIF, and Constitutional AI. The paper sketches a care-informed feedback example but does not develop a full technical method or report an original empirical evaluation.
data_sources: Cited scholarship on ethics of care and moral psychology
Cited research and reports on neural-network generalization and AI bias
Descriptions of RLHF, RLAIF, and Constitutional AI
methodology.sample_or_scope: LLM development and value alignment, particularly applications involving care and vulnerability
analysis_methods: Normative comparison of care ethics with utilitarian and justice-based approaches
Argument from generalization failures and reported bias cases
Conceptual analysis of feedback-based alignment mechanisms

assumptions.text: The authors' proposal presumes that alignment processes can be adapted to recognize morally salient individual and relational features, even though they do not specify a complete implementation.

limitations.text: The paper does not provide a comprehensive technical methodology for implementing care-based value alignment.
Care ethics resists formalization and lacks easily codifiable principles, complicating its implementation in machine-learning architectures built around abstraction and generalization.

Current LLMs lack genuine understanding of vulnerability, dependency, and relational dynamics, and their capacity to recognize and respond to complex emotional and social cues remains technically underdeveloped.
The claimed benefits of care-based alignment, including reduced sycophancy and hallucinations, are predictions rather than outcomes demonstrated by a care-aligned system in this paper.

proposed_solutions.text: Adapt LLM design and alignment strategies to accommodate care ethics' attention to relationality, vulnerability, and contextual particularities.
Modify RLHF or RLAIF to interpret and reinforce feedback in light of individual and contextual moral significance rather than generic reward maximization.
In a mental-health chatbot, train the model to identify vulnerability, dependency, or self-harm cues and adjust its response to the user's emotional state, expressed needs, empathy, and safety.
Bring care-based considerations into human labeling and constitutional approaches, accounting for relational impacts and the well-being of both caregivers and care-receivers.
Pursue interdisciplinary research and cautious implementation when incorporating care ethics into AI design.

open_questions.text: How can the contextual and relational principles of care ethics be operationalized as a full technical value alignment method?
How can LLMs recognize and respond meaningfully to vulnerability, dependency, and complex emotional or social cues despite their currently underdeveloped capacities?
